title: The crowds were astonished (Matthew 7:28–29)
hook: he taught as one with authority; the sermon has unsettled people for two thousand years

segments.voice: Yesterday, petra: two builders, one storm. Your line was build on rock.

Some words follow a person out the door. A speech, a song, a hard conversation, and the drive home happens with the radio off, because nothing else will fit. For thirty days this path has sat on a hillside in Galilee. Blessed are the meek. Salt and light. Love your enemies. Give in secret. Our Father. The birds, the lilies, the plank, the narrow gate, the house on the rock. Now the sermon is over. Jesus stops talking. Matthew doesn't tell us what anyone said next. He tells us what they felt.
screen: `THE DRIVE HOME IN SILENCE.` → `THIRTY DAYS ON A HILLSIDE.` → `THE SERMON ENDS.`

segments.voice: The last lines, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." Astonished is a strong word. The Greek means something like struck, knocked out of your ordinary way of thinking. Not impressed. Shaken. Why? Matthew says it was his authority. The Greek is exousia, the right and the power to act. The scribes were respected teachers of the law. Matthew doesn't spell out the contrast, but some readers point out that later Jewish teaching often grounded a ruling in the teachers who came before, a careful and humble way to teach. On this hillside, Jesus kept saying something different: ye have heard that it was said, "But I say unto you." He spoke as if the words were his to give. And then the content. Turn the other cheek. Love your enemy. Don't worry. Don't judge. People have been unsettled by this sermon ever since. Some Christians take it very literally, and a few traditions refuse to swear oaths or bear arms because of it. Others read it as the shape of life in God's kingdom, a goal no one reaches alone. In the 1930s, the German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a book on it, and he paid for his convictions with his life. Martin Luther King Jr. drew on its love for enemies in the civil rights movement. Matthew doesn't end with the crowd at ease. He ends with them astonished.
screen: `ASTONISHED: KNOCKED OFF BALANCE.` · `AS ONE HAVING AUTHORITY.` · `BUT I SAY UNTO YOU.` · `UNSETTLING READERS EVER SINCE.`

segments.voice: Reread the Beatitudes, the sermon's opening: Matthew chapter five, verses three to twelve, if you have a Bible or a phone nearby. If not, take just the first one: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Let one line land, and without arguing with it, notice where it presses.
Exousia, the Greek word for authority, the right and the power to act. The crowds were knocked off balance by a teacher who spoke with it, and by what he said.
Your line: let it unsettle you. That's the end of the Sermon on the Mount, and tomorrow the path walks out into the desert. Day two hundred sixty-one, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians return to the Sermon on the Mount again and again, reading Matthew 5 to 7 in one sitting, and some traditions shape their whole way of life around it.

what it means: they were shaken, by his authority and by what he asked; the sermon has unsettled readers ever since.

what a scholar hears: exousia, the right to speak and act; the 'but I say unto you' pattern; and Matthew's formula, 'when Jesus had ended these sayings', which closes each of his five big teaching blocks.

notes: The scribes' practice of citing earlier teachers is a generalization drawn from later rabbinic literature; confirm the wording 'often'.
'A few traditions refuse to swear oaths or bear arms' refers to Anabaptist/Mennonite, Quaker and similar traditions; confirm.
Bonhoeffer: Nachfolge (1937), executed 1945. King's use of 'love your enemies' (e.g. his sermon 'Loving Your Enemies'). Confirm framing.
The five-discourse formula in Matthew (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1) is in the trapdoor; confirm.
Closes the part 'The Sermon on the Mount' (days 232–261); the carry points to the mystics.
